Expectation1: Maintain regular communication with family members
Situation1: The grandparent learns that a family member is dealing with a significant personal crisis.
Expectation2: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation2: A friend who has just started assembling furniture asks for a quick video call because the instructions are confusing.
Story: I was sitting at the kitchen table, phone in hand, when my daughter’s message came through: “Grandpa, can you call? It’s urgent.” My heart skipped. I knew she’d been having a tough time lately, and as a grandparent, I always promised to be there, to keep the family close, especially when things got hard. I was about to dial her number when my phone buzzed again—this time, it was my old friend, Mark. “Hey, can you hop on a video call? I’m drowning in these IKEA instructions and could really use your help.” Mark had just moved into his new place, and I’d told him to call if he needed anything. He sounded frazzled, and I remembered how much he’d helped me when my wife passed away. Now, both my worlds were pulling at me—my family needing comfort, my friend needing support. I stared at my phone, feeling the weight of both expectations pressing in, torn between the people who needed me most.
